study_identification_part.si4_title: Multiscale Heterogeneity of White Matter Morphometry in Psychiatric Disorders

study_characteristics_part.sc1_study_objective: To apply normative modeling to T1-weighted MRI data to map interindividual variability in person-specific white matter volume (WMV) deviations in psychiatric disorders and characterize deviation heterogeneity across multiple spatial scales from individual voxels through interregional connections, brain regions, and spatially extended brain networks.

rci9_site_effect_handling.detail: Site/scanner effects were handled within the normative model by including scan site as a covariate in the warped Bayesian linear regression model. B-spline basis expansion over age was used to model non-linear effects, and likelihood warping was used to model non-Gaussian and heteroscedastic imaging phenotypes. The model's efficacy in removing site effects was validated using linear support vector machines trained on deviation z-maps to classify scan sites. Balanced accuracy scores ranged between 49.71% and 58.53% (close to 50% chance level), indicating successful removal of site-related variance. Both linear and non-linear site effects were adequately addressed.

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa7_association_analysis: Deviation burden comparisons between clinical and control groups using nonparametric rank sum tests (Mann-Whitney U test, one-tailed). For spatial overlap analysis: permutation testing (10,000 permutations) with generalized Pareto tail approximation to test for differences in the proportion of individuals showing extreme deviations at each voxel, connection, region, and network between cases and controls; FDR correction (pFDR < .05, two-tailed) applied for multiple comparisons. Analyses conducted separately for positive and negative deviations. Multi-scale analysis framework: voxel-level, tract-level (dysconnectome matrices showing affected pairwise connections), region-level (gray matter regions attached to affected tracts), and network-level (10 canonical functional networks from Yeo parcellation plus 3 subcortical groups; sensitivity analysis with 20-network parcellation). Support vector machine classification used to evaluate site effect removal (balanced accuracy scores). Sensitivity analyses with different extreme deviation thresholds (z < -2.6, -1.96, -1.65) and cluster sizes (10, 50 voxels).
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa8_key_findings_brief: Extreme white matter volume deviations showed high voxel-level heterogeneity across all disorders (maximum overlap <5% negative, <8% positive), but for ASD and SCZ, these heterogeneous deviations aggregated within common tracts, regions, and functional networks affecting up to 69% of individuals, while other disorders showed no significant regional or network aggregation.
clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa9_key_findings_detailed: At the voxel level, no voxel showed extreme negative deviations in more than 5% of individuals with the same diagnosis, and positive deviations affected no more than 8%, indicating high spatial heterogeneity. Only 21.56% of controls showed at least one negative extreme deviation, compared to 13.17% (OCD) to 35.77% (SCZ) for cases; positive deviations were more common, with 60.59% of controls and 50.93% (MDD) to 71.78% (ASD) of cases affected. ASD and SCZ showed significantly higher median negative deviation burden than controls (p<.001), and ASD also showed higher positive deviation burden (p=.001). At the tract level, maximum overlap ranged from 4.19% (OCD) to 15.40% (SCZ) vs. 8.18% in controls. ASD showed greater overlap in tracts linking visual areas and amygdala; SCZ showed greater overlap in somatomotor-thalamic connections (pFDR<.05). At the region level, ASD and SCZ showed significantly greater overlap than controls in 86% and 91% of regions, respectively (pFDR<.05). At the network level, ASD and SCZ showed greater overlap than controls in all 10 functional networks for negative deviations (pFDR<.05), with maximum overlap of 31.68% (ASD) and 35.77% (SCZ) vs. 19.70% in controls; 32% of ASD and 35% of SCZ individuals with extreme negative deviations and 69% of ASD individuals with extreme positive deviations showed involvement of nearly all networks. OCD showed significantly less network overlap than controls (pFDR<.05). No significant differences were found for ADHD, BP, or MDD at any spatial scale after FDR correction. The results were robust to different threshold choices (z<-1.96, -1.65; cluster sizes 10, 50 voxels). Fewer individuals showed negative WMV deviations (≤36%) compared to previous GMV findings (76% in the same cohort), suggesting WMV may be relatively spared in psychiatric illness.

caa10_key_limitations.answer: WMV quantification using VBM-derived Jacobian does not account for white matter fiber orientation dependence (changes perpendicular vs. along fibers have different functional implications); diffusion MRI tractography has well-documented limitations including false positives/negatives in complex fiber architecture (crossing, branching fibers); DSM-based diagnoses are clinical heuristics with limitations including comorbidity and within-group heterogeneity; group differences in total deviation burden can drive overlap differences, complicating inferences about specific targeting (lacks appropriate null models for WMV as exist for GMV); inability to determine whether positive WMV deviations reflect true biology or model limitations in capturing nonlinearities; transdiagnostic symptom-based approaches may yield more precise deviation mappings than diagnostic categories.
caa10_key_limitations.supporting_text: The quantification of WMV deviations was based on our previous work on GMV deviations using the Jacobian of the nonlinear warp field. However, unlike gray matter, white matter's fibrous bundles have a strong orientation dependence... diffusion MRI struggles to accurately reconstruct tracts in voxels with complex fiber architecture... Diagnoses that are based on nosological systems such as the DSM (37) are clinical heuristics that do not necessarily define biological entities, with several well-documented limitations including pervasive comorbidity (60) and within-group clinical heterogeneity (11)... Group differences in total deviation burden can drive differences in group overlap, thereby complicating inferences about specific targeting of connections, regions, or networks. While GMV studies have methods to address this (22), WMV analyses lack such null models... It remains unclear whether this increase in WMV is a true biological phenomenon or a limitation of current normative models in capturing nonlinearities in the voxelwise WMV estimates... Focusing on syndromes or symptoms that cut across diagnostic boundaries (65) may yield more precise mappings of voxelwise deviations

clinical_application_and_analysis_part.caa11_application_notes: The study developed a novel multiscale framework for characterizing deviation heterogeneity across four spatial resolutions: voxel-level (traditional normative modeling output), tract-level (dysconnectome matrices mapping affected white matter connections), region-level (gray matter regions connected to affected tracts), and network-level (canonical functional networks from Yeo parcellation). This framework bridges individual-level heterogeneity with systems-level convergence. The tract-level analysis used an independent high-quality diffusion tractography dataset (HCP150) rather than the clinical samples themselves, following the logic of lesion network mapping studies. For the dysconnectome analysis, streamlines from the HCP150 cohort were filtered by each individual's WMV deviation maps, and consensus matrices were created by aggregating across HCP150 individuals (with 50% or 75% weight thresholds) to account for inter-individual variability in normative connectome architecture. The paper explicitly compares WMV and GMV deviation prevalence in the same cohort (from their previous publication), finding lower WMV deviation burden. Sex-stratified analyses are mentioned as a direction for future work but not performed here (though sex is included as a model covariate). The study is limited to adults aged 18-64 years.

general_note_part.gn1_general_notes: This study is a companion to Segal et al. 2023 (Nature Neuroscience) which examined gray matter volume deviations in the same cohort. The current study extends that work to white matter, allowing direct comparison of GMV vs. WMV deviation patterns. The paper notes that WMV deviations are less prevalent than GMV deviations previously reported in the same sample (≤36% vs. 76% showing at least one extreme negative deviation). The study emphasizes that the extreme voxel-level heterogeneity observed (maximum 5% overlap) challenges group-mean case-control paradigms but demonstrates that heterogeneous deviations can aggregate at coarser spatial scales (tracts, regions, networks) particularly in ASD and SCZ. The HCP150 tractography cohort was used for all participants to map structural connectivity because high-quality diffusion data was not available for all clinical samples. An important methodological note: the paper reports median rather than mean age for all demographic summaries, which is unusual for normative modeling studies. The analysis framework considers both positive and negative deviations separately throughout, with positive deviations being more prevalent but showing fewer significant case-control differences. The study notes that better null models are needed for WMV to disentangle effects of deviation burden vs. specific anatomical targeting. All data came from previously published datasets with varying acquisition parameters (see Table S1 in Segal et al. 2023 for detailed scanner specifications). Ethics approval was obtained from Monash University Research Ethics Committee (Project ID: 23534) as well as local ethics committees for each contributing dataset. Data processing was conducted using the Multi-modal Australian ScienceS Imaging and Visualization Environment (MASSIVE) HPC facility. A preprint version was previously published on bioRxiv (2024.08.04.606523v1).
